1 Introduction

TODO: introduce the dataset/paper, maybe briefly talk about how/why the dataset was chosen

This report describes the selection, data preparation, normalization, and differential expression analysis of a publicly available human gene expression dataset. TODO: The workflow follows best practices for RNA-seq analysis as outlined by Dawadi et al. (2025) (dawadi_bench_2025?)

1.1 Dataset Selection

TODO: brief description The selected dataset is GSE166605 from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO). This RNA-seq dataset investigates TODO: [transcriptional responses of human CD14+ monocytes under experimentally defined conditions involving differential treatment exposure]. The dataset was chosen because TODO The selected dataset is GSE166605 from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO). This RNA-seq dataset investigates the transcriptional responses of human CD14+ monocytes. Specifically, it analyzes the effect of miR-155 overexpression compared to a negative control.

This dataset is of interest because miR-155 is a critical regulator of immune function and inflammation. Understanding its downstream targets in monocytes can reveal mechanisms of immune activation.

A detailed account of the dataset discovery process is documented separately here.

1.2 Dataset Background

  • paper background(Olsson et al. (2022))

  • TODO: control and test conditions of dataset Organism: Homo sapiens

Tissue: CD14+ Monocytes

Control Condition: Negative Control (Neg_C)

Test Condition: miR-155 Overexpression (miR_155)

2 Data Exploration & Clean-up

The following sections describes initial steps in the analysis, from accessing the dataset to cleaning the data and performing preliminary exploratory analysis.

First, necessary libraries were installed (if necessary) and loaded into the R session.

2.1 Obtaining the Data

The dataset was accessed and downloaded using GEOquery and the corresponding GEO series ID. The raw count data file was downloaded programmatically in R without manual file management, to ensure reproducibility of results. To ensure reproducibility while avoiding repeated downloads, files are only retrieved if not already present locally in designated data files directory.

TODO:make pretty: Below is a snapshot of the raw matrix:

GSE_ID <- "GSE166605" # constant for GEO series ID to reduce risk of accessing the wrong dataset
data_dir <- "A1_files"

# checking for existence of directory for storing data files
if (!dir.exists(data_dir)) 
  dir.create(data_dir)

counts_file <- file.path(data_dir, "GSE166605_D1-5_Neg_C_miR_155_RAW_counts.txt.gz")

# access raw files from GEO if the file(s) weren't previously downloaded
if (!file.exists(counts_file)) {
  GEOquery::getGEOSuppFiles(GSE_ID,
                            makeDirectory = FALSE,
                            baseDir = data_dir)
}

# read in raw count file: columns are samples and rows are genes
raw_counts <- readr::read_tsv(counts_file, show_col_types = FALSE)

# names(raw_counts)[1:min(12, ncol(raw_counts))]  # TODO: remove
# preview raw count data
kable_head(raw_counts, caption = "Preview of Raw Count Data from GEO") # TODO:make sure it renders decently/pretty

TODO: Add comments explaining: - Why raw counts are required for edgeR - Why integers are necessary (NB distribution assumption)(?)

# processing count file to only contain expression values (remove GeneID and Gene Name columns)
counts <- raw_counts %>%
  dplyr::select(starts_with("D")) %>% # based on GEO accession page, all sample names start with 'D'
  as.data.frame()

rownames(counts) <- raw_counts$GeneID

counts <- as.matrix(counts) # converted to matrix for compatibility with DE analysis packages

# check that all values in the counts matrix are *mathematically* integers (even if the storage type isn't) before converting storage type of count values to integers
stopifnot(all(counts %% 1 == 0))
storage.mode(counts) <- "integer"

samples <- colnames(counts)[1:ncol(counts)]
cell_line  <- unlist(lapply(samples,FUN =
                             function(x){unlist(strsplit(x,split = " "))[2]}))       
treatment <- unlist(lapply(samples,FUN = 
                             function(x){unlist(strsplit(x,split = " "))[3]}))     
meta_df <- data.frame(samples, cell_line, treatment)

2.2 Gene ID mapping

# helper function to remove Ensembl IDs' version numbers:
strip_ensembl_version <- function(x) sub("\\..*$", "", x)

mapped_counts <- data.frame(ensembl_gene_id = rownames(counts),
                            counts)

mapped_counts$ensembl_gene_id <- strip_ensembl_version(mapped_counts$ensembl_gene_id)
# TODO: check for duplicate ensembl IDs now that version numbers have been stripped

ensembl <- biomaRt::useMart("ensembl", dataset = "hsapiens_gene_ensembl") # using latest Human Genes mart
map <- biomaRt::getBM(
  #attributes should include both ensembl gene ID and hgnc symbol to ensure we can map back to the ensembl gene in the original data from hgnc at any point in our analysis 
  attributes = c("ensembl_gene_id", "hgnc_symbol"),
  filters = "ensembl_gene_id",
  values = mapped_counts$ensembl_gene_id,
  mart = ensembl
)

# TODO: remove?
# kable_head(map, 10, paste(": mapping preview"))

counts_mapped <- mapped_counts %>%
  left_join(map, by = "ensembl_gene_id") %>%
dplyr::select(ensembl_gene_id,hgnc_symbol, everything())

3 Data Normalization

Prior to differential expression analysis, I performed Trimmed Mean of M-values (TMM) normalization (Robinson and Oshlack (2010)) on the cleaned count data. 3.1`

5 Discussion

  1. Why is the dataset of interest to you?
  2. What are the control and test conditions of the dataset?
  3. How many samples in each of the conditions of your dataset?
  4. Were there expression values that were not unique for specific genes? How did you handle these?
  5. Were there expression values that could not be mapped to current HUGO symbols?
  6. Were there any outliers in your dataset? How were they handled in the originating paper? How many outliers were removed?
  7. How did you handle replicates?
  8. What is the final coverage of your dataset?

Additional “rough work”/trial code and reflections can be found here.
